doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Being an asset to your community
summary: He tells students to be an asset to any community, from Carnegie Hall to funerals, and dislikes wedding coordinators.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: I don’t know that sounds fishy to me.

It is. And you know it was great because I felt like that was a good function for — and I bought some records occasionally you know and stuff like that. But mostly I used it to feel like I was helping with the family stuff you know. And I think that’s a good — and I tell students this all the time. I say, “Look, the most important thing is to be an asset to your community.” I say “It doesn’t matter if you’re on Carnegie Hall stage that’s a community. Make sure you’re doing what is necessary to be an asset to that group. If you’re playing with a junior high school or conducting a junior high school band make sure you’re an asset to that community. If somebody dies in your community and you can play at the service and you know that person especially, you can volunteer to play.” I still do it. You know? Because when they finish that service invariably people will come up to me and say, “Oh my gosh when you played the ‘Ave Maria’ it really helped the whole where I was.” You know? And you go what could be better than that? That’s real. You go on, you know I go play with some orchestra let’s say, and I love playing with orchestras. And I played in Carnegie Hall a lot of times. And I even played solos with the Cincinnati Pops in Carnegie Hall. And you know the whole time you’re there you see these people just — remember when — I’m thinking well I like Haydn’s Concerto but I think Joe Smith, you know, I like the way he plays it better. They’re not there for the record, they don’t have any — but you know somebody who you’ve touched in a situation like a funeral, a wedding. I don’t do weddings anymore, I hate wedding coordinators. They’re awful. But you know they tell you what to do and I say, “I’m not doing that. I’m not going to stand where the bride is supposed to come out and play from there. Do you want everybody to look at me before they look at the bride? It isn’t going to happen.” With her dad, you know what I’m saying?
